```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A Shiny app can query Oracle Database using the signed-in visitor's
permissions. This lets you use the database's existing access rules when
building a dashboard or reporting app.

`oauth_db_oracle()` opens a DBI connection for SQL and dbplyr. Oracle checks
the visitor's access token and maps their identity to database privileges.
Your administrator must configure that mapping before the app can connect.
For access over HTTPS without an Oracle driver, see
[Oracle REST Data Services](oracle-ords.html).

## Set up the database and driver

Install `odbc` in R and Oracle Instant Client's **Basic** and **ODBC**
packages for your R architecture. Register the driver, then find its name
with `odbc::odbcListDrivers()`. Check the
[ODBC setup guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/odbcd/using-oracle-database-odbc-driver.html)
for a client version compatible with your database's OAuth integration.

Your administrator needs to configure Oracle to trust the sign-in provider
and map users to database privileges. This example uses Oracle Deep Data
Security direct logon, which gives the database an end-user identity.
The authorization models and provider-specific setup follow the app.

Ask for an encrypted connection's host, port and service name. If the
database needs an Oracle wallet or a particular server certificate name,
get those settings too.

## Register the Shiny application

Register an authorization-code client with PKCE at the provider trusted
by the database. Register `http://localhost:8100` as its redirect URI.
The app needs the database access scope and the corresponding user or
group assignments. Configure the provider to issue the database audience
and required identity and role claims. For Keycloak, configure an audience
mapper and a top-level role claim matching Oracle's provider configuration.

The complete app below uses OIDC discovery for a Keycloak or OCI IAM
Identity Domains provider with OpenID Connect enabled. Its `"end_user"`
mode requires Oracle Deep Data Security direct logon. Enable refresh-token
issuance when requesting `offline_access`, or replace that scope with your
provider's documented refresh setup. An Entra alternative follows the app.

Save the app settings in your local `.Renviron` and restart R:

```text
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-shiny-app-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-shiny-app-client-secret
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_ISSUER=https://login.example.org/realms/reporting
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SCOPE=database.read
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_HOST=database.example.org
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SERVICE=reporting.example.org
OAUTHDB_ORACLE_DRIVER=Oracle in instantclient_19_30
```

| Setting | Where to find it |
| --- | --- |
| `OAUTHDB_ORACLE_ISSUER` | OIDC issuer configured for the database's provider |
| `OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SCOPE` | Exact database access scope supplied by the administrator; OCI IAM uses the resource audience concatenated with the scope name |
| Host, service and TCPS port | Oracle connection details supplied by the administrator |
| Driver | Installed driver name reported by `odbc::odbcListDrivers()` |
| Wallet and certificate DN, if needed | Oracle administrator's TLS configuration |

## A complete app

The app first displays the Oracle end-user identity. Save it as
`example.R`, using your database's connection settings:

After signing in,
click **Load rows**. The app starts its workers once and stops them at shutdown.

```{r app}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

scope <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SCOPE")

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_ISSUER")
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "offline_access", scope),
  required_scopes = scope
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),

    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),

  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )

  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_oracle(
    auth$connection,
    host = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_HOST"),
    service_name = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_SERVICE"),
    driver = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_DRIVER"),
    port = 1522L,
    authorization_model = "end_user"
  )

  query_task <- oauth_db_task(con)

  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke(
      "SELECT ORA_END_USER_CONTEXT.username AS database_user FROM DUAL"
    )
  })

  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*", onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)

    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at its registered redirect URI.
```

Save the code as `example.R`, set your TCPS port and any wallet or
certificate DN arguments, then run `source("example.R")`. Open
`http://localhost:8100` in your regular browser and sign in. The example
shows the Oracle end-user identity. Replace the query with a table or view
the user can read.

## Choose an Oracle authorization model

The model must match the database configuration:

| Model | What Oracle establishes | Helper argument |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global schema | A global database user mapped to the external identity | `authorization_model = "global"` (the default) |
| End-user context | An individual identity for Deep Data Security policies | `authorization_model = "end_user"` |

The app above uses end-user context. For a global-schema deployment, change
the argument and query `SELECT USER FROM DUAL` to inspect the database user.

Provider setup depends on the Oracle release and deployment:

| Provider | Database configuration |
| --- | --- |
| Microsoft Entra | Follow the [Entra integration guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dbseg/configuring-oracle-database-microsoft-entra-id-integration.html) and its [client support table](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/dbseg/supported-client-drivers-entra-ad-connections.html) |
| OCI IAM Identity Domains | Configure [OCI IAM OAuth](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/refrn/IDENTITY_PROVIDER_OAUTH_CONFIG.html), available from Oracle 26ai RU 23.26.2 |
| Keycloak | Use Oracle 26ai's [Deep Data Security provider configuration](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/ddscg/configure-database-iam-integration.html) and [direct-logon setup](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/ddscg/configure-sql-client-end-user-direct-logon.html); this integration isn't available on Autonomous Database |

For OCI IAM OAuth, supply the administrator's server certificate name as
`server_cert_dn`. If the service requires mutual TLS, also supply its
wallet directory as `wallet_location`. Other deployments can use the
client's configured trust store or an Oracle wallet; see `?oauth_db_oracle`.

## Microsoft Entra alternative

For Entra, use the Microsoft client with a custom database resource target.
Register a **Web** application with the same redirect URI and the database's
delegated permission, commonly `session:scope:connect`. Your administrator
must configure global-schema or data-role mappings and access-token claims;
Entra v2 setup includes the `upn` claim. See Oracle's
[registration example](https://docs.oracle.com/en/learn/ocidb-auth-msentraid/)
and [Microsoft app registration](azure-sql.html#register-a-microsoft-entra-app).

```{r entra-client}
resource <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ORACLE_RESOURCE")
scope <- paste0(resource, "/session:scope:connect")

client <- oauth_db_microsoft_client(
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  token_targets = list(
    oracle = list(resource = resource, scopes = scope, required_scopes = scope)
  )
)
```

`OAUTHDB_ORACLE_RESOURCE` is the database server's Entra Application ID URI,
not the Shiny application's client ID. In the app's connection helper, set
`target = "oracle"`. For an existing global-schema deployment, set
`authorization_model = "global"` and query `SELECT USER FROM DUAL` to
inspect the database schema identity. For Deep Data Security use
`authorization_model = "end_user"` and retain the end-user identity query.
Use the exact granted database scope in `required_scopes`; keep
`/.default` in the client's consent settings.

## Connections and token files

Call `con()` before each operation. Global-schema connections stay open
through ordinary token renewal. End-user connections reopen when the token
changes, so the database receives updated role claims. Sign-out, account
changes and session end close both types.

The helper verifies the selected authorization model when connecting. An
end-user connection requires Oracle to establish the matching end-user
context; a successful global-schema login alone isn't sufficient.

The Oracle driver receives the token through a temporary file, which the
helper removes after connecting. On Windows, keep R's temporary directory
private to the app's operating-system user. If a connection breaks, call
`con()` to reopen it with a current token. See `?oauth_db_oracle` for driver,
wallet and token-file settings.
